subject: Mathematics
title: Kavya's Dance: Motion, Force, and Direction
hook: A dancer discovers how vectors describe both position and movement on stage

slides.title: Vector Algebra
slides.storyContext: Kavya practices Bharatanatyam in her studio. Every move has direction and magnitude—steps, turns, hand movements. Her choreographer Ramesh says, 'This is vector algebra,' and Kavya's eyes light up.

slides.title: The Choreography Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ramesh is choreographing a group dance. He needs to describe where each dancer should move. He tells Kavya, 'Start at center. Move 3 meters east, then 4 meters north. Where do you end up?' Kavya thinks: 'That's not just about distance—it's about direction too!' Ramesh's brother Pradeep, a physics teacher, hears this and says, 'That's vector addition!' He shows them how vectors make dance positioning precise.

slides.title: Scalars and Vectors
slides.storyContext: Pradeep draws on a board: 'A scalar is just a number—like distance traveled (5 km). A vector has both magnitude and direction—like displacement (5 km north).'

points.label: Scalar
points.text: Quantity with magnitude only. Examples: distance (5 m), mass (70 kg), temperature (37°C).

points.label: Vector
points.text: Quantity with magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement (5 m north), velocity (20 m/s east), force (10 N downward).

points.label: Notation
points.text: Vectors are written as →AB or boldface v, or with arrow: $\vec{v}$. Magnitude is |→v| or just v.

points.label: Components
points.text: In 2D, vector v is written as v = (vₓ, vᵧ) or v = vₓ î + vᵧ ĵ, where î, ĵ are unit vectors along x, y axes.

example.problem: Kavya's first move: 3 meters east, 4 meters north. Using axes (east=x, north=y), displacement vector d = (3, 4) or d = 3î + 4ĵ. Magnitude |d| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 meters. Direction: angle θ = arctan(4/3) ≈ 53.1° from east.
example.solution: Her displacement is a vector of magnitude 5 m at 53.1° north of east. She ends up 5 meters away from center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scalars are just numbers; vectors have size and direction. Use components to calculate exact positions.

slides.title: Why Magnitude Matters
slides.storyContext: Kavya asks Pradeep, 'If I move 3 meters east and then 4 meters north, did I really travel 7 meters from the start?' Pradeep smiles. 'No, the shortest path is 5 meters. That's the magnitude of the displacement vector. You traveled 7 meters along the path, but your net displacement is 5 meters.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Distance (path length) and displacement (net vector) are different. Vectors capture the net effect, not the path.

slides.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Kavya makes a second move: 2 meters west, 1 meter south. Ramesh asks, 'What's your total displacement?' This requires adding vectors.

points.label: Component addition
points.text: If u = (uₓ, uᵧ) and v = (vₓ, vᵧ), then u + v = (uₓ + vₓ, uᵧ + vᵧ).

points.label: Graphical method
points.text: Place tail of second vector at head of first; resultant goes from tail of first to head of second (triangle/parallelogram rule).

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: u - v = u + (-v). Vector -v has same magnitude but opposite direction.

example.problem: Kavya's first move: d₁ = (3, 4). Second move: 2 meters west (−2 m, 0), 1 meter south (0, −1), so d₂ = (−2, −1). Total displacement: d = d₁ + d₂ = (3, 4) + (−2, −1) = (1, 3). Magnitude: |d| = √(1² + 3²) = √10 ≈ 3.16 meters. Direction: θ = arctan(3/1) ≈ 71.6° from east.
example.solution: After both moves, Kavya is 3.16 meters away from center, at about 71.6° north of east.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add vectors by adding their components separately. Subtract by adding the negative vector.

slides.title: Adding Three Vectors in Dance
slides.storyContext: Ramesh choreographs a triple-step: first 2 meters south, then 3 meters east, then 1 meter north. Find total displacement.

example.problem: Step 1: v₁ = (0, −2). Step 2: v₂ = (3, 0). Step 3: v₃ = (0, 1). Total: v = v₁ + v₂ + v₃ = (0+3+0, −2+0+1) = (3, −1). Magnitude: |v| = √(9+1) = √10 ≈ 3.16 m. Direction: θ = arctan(−1/3) ≈ −18.4° (south of east).
example.solution: Kavya ends 3.16 meters away from start, roughly 18° south of east.

slides.inSimpleWords: To add multiple vectors, add all x-components and all y-components separately.

slides.title: Finding the Middle Ground
slides.storyContext: Pradeep asks Kavya to find the midpoint between two stage positions: A = (2, 3) and B = (8, 7). Kavya thinks, 'That's the average of the positions!' She calculates M = ((2+8)/2, (3+7)/2) = (5, 5).
slides.inSimpleWords: Midpoint of two vectors = average of their components. Useful for centering choreography.

slides.title: Dot Product (Scalar Product)
slides.storyContext: Pradeep introduces the dot product: 'This tells us how much two vectors align or point in the same direction.' Ramesh uses this to calculate work in a dance lift.

points.label: Definition
points.text: For vectors u = (uₓ, uᵧ, u_z) and v = (vₓ, vᵧ, v_z), dot product u·v = uₓvₓ + uᵧvᵧ + u_zv_z.

points.label: Geometric form
points.text: u·v = |u| |v| cos(θ), where θ is angle between vectors.

points.label: Properties
points.text: u·v = v·u (commutative). If θ = 90°, then u·v = 0 (perpendicular vectors have zero dot product).

points.label: Work in physics
points.text: Work W = F·d = |F| |d| cos(θ), where F is force, d is displacement.

example.problem: In a dance lift, Pradeep models a dancer (Kavya) and partner (another performer). Force applied by partner: F = (40, 30, 10) N (x, y, z components). Displacement of Kavya: d = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) m. Work = F·d = 40(0.5) + 30(0.3) + 10(0.2) = 20 + 9 + 2 = 31 joules.
example.solution: Work done in the lift is 31 joules. Since this is positive, the lift raises Kavya successfully.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dot product measures how two vectors align. Multiply corresponding components and add them up.

slides.title: Perpendicular Movements
slides.storyContext: Kavya moves 5 meters east (vector u = (5, 0)). Then Ramesh asks her to move perpendicular to that—directly north (vector v = (0, 4)). She calculates: u · v = 5(0) + 0(4) = 0. Pradeep nods: 'When dot product is zero, the vectors are perpendicular. No overlap in direction.'
slides.inSimpleWords: If dot product = 0, vectors are perpendicular (90° angle). Otherwise they have an angle between 0° and 180°.

slides.title: Cross Product (Vector Product)
slides.storyContext: Pradeep says, 'The cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both original vectors. In dance, this describes rotation or torque.' Ramesh uses it for spinning moves.

points.label: Definition (3D)
points.text: u × v = (uᵧv_z − u_zv_y, u_zv_x − uₓv_z, uₓv_y − uᵧv_x). Written as determinant: u × v = | î  ĵ  k̂ | | uₓ uᵧ u_z | | vₓ vᵧ v_z |

points.label: Magnitude
points.text: |u × v| = |u| |v| sin(θ), where θ is angle between u and v.

points.label: Direction
points.text: u × v is perpendicular to both u and v. Direction given by right-hand rule: curl fingers from u to v; thumb points in direction of u × v.

points.label: Torque
points.text: Torque τ = r × F, where r is position vector, F is force. Magnitude tells how strongly rotation occurs.

example.problem: Kavya spins around a vertical axis. Her position from axis: r = (2, 0, 0) meters. Force applied (by her muscles): F = (0, 10, 5) N. Torque: τ = r × F. Using determinant formula: τ = | î  ĵ  k̂ | | 2  0  0 | | 0 10 5 | = î(0×5 − 0×10) − ĵ(2×5 − 0×0) + k̂(2×10 − 0×0) = 0î − 10ĵ + 20k̂ = (0, −10, 20). Magnitude: |τ| = √(0² + 10² + 20²) = √500 ≈ 22.4 N·m.
example.solution: Torque is about 22.4 N·m pointing mostly upward (positive z), causing clockwise spin when viewed from above.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cross product gives a perpendicular vector. Its magnitude shows how strongly two vectors 'rotate' around each other.

slides.title: Cross Product in 2D (Special Case)
slides.storyContext: When working in 2D (the stage floor), Pradeep shows Kavya how to use the 2D version: u × v = uₓvᵧ − uᵧvₓ (gives a scalar).

example.problem: Kavya's displacement u = (3, 4) (east and north). Her velocity v = (1, 2) m/s. 2D cross product: u × v = 3(2) − 4(1) = 6 − 4 = 2. This value indicates rotational tendency on the floor plane.
example.solution: Positive result shows counter-clockwise rotation tendency. The magnitude 2 tells the strength.

slides.inSimpleWords: In 2D, cross product becomes a scalar: uₓvᵧ − uᵧvₓ. It's useful for detecting rotation direction.

slides.title: Using Angles to Measure Alignment
slides.storyContext: Pradeep teaches Kavya to use angles: 'The dot product formula u·v = |u| |v| cos(θ) tells us the angle between two movements. If θ = 0°, they're perfectly aligned (moving same way). If θ = 90°, perpendicular. If θ = 180°, opposite.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Dot product and angle are connected. Use cos(θ) to find how much vectors align.

slides.title: Unit Vectors and Direction Cosines
slides.storyContext: Pradeep teaches Kavya how to describe exact directions. 'A unit vector points in a direction with length 1. Use it as a compass.'

points.label: Unit vector
points.text: u-hat = u / |u| gives unit vector in direction of u.

points.label: Direction cosines
points.text: For vector v making angles α, β, γ with x, y, z axes: cos(α), cos(β), cos(γ) are direction cosines. cos²(α) + cos²(β) + cos²(γ) = 1.

points.label: Standard basis
points.text: î = (1, 0, 0), ĵ = (0, 1, 0), k̂ = (0, 0, 1) are unit vectors along coordinate axes.

example.problem: Kavya's displacement d = (3, 4) meters. Find unit vector in this direction. |d| = 5. Unit vector: d-hat = (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8). Direction cosines (2D): cos(α) = 0.6 (angle from x-axis ≈ 53.1°), cos(β) = 0.8 (angle from y-axis ≈ 36.9°). Verify: 0.6² + 0.8² = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1. ✓
example.solution: Unit vector is (0.6, 0.8). This tells exactly which way Kavya is facing after her first displacement.

slides.inSimpleWords: Unit vectors and direction cosines give precise compass directions for any displacement.

slides.title: Finding the Direction of Motion
slides.storyContext: Ramesh describes Kavya's movement as displacement v = (6, 8). She wonders, 'What's the direction in degrees?' Pradeep helps: magnitude |v| = 10, unit vector = (0.6, 0.8). This means 60% of the motion is east, 80% is north.
slides.inSimpleWords: Unit vectors break down a displacement into directional components that sum (via Pythagoras) to magnitude 1.

slides.title: Collinear and Coplanar Vectors
slides.storyContext: Pradeep explores relationships between vectors. 'Some vectors lie on the same line (collinear). Others fit in the same plane (coplanar). How do we detect this?'

points.label: Collinear vectors
points.text: Vectors u and v are collinear if one is a scalar multiple of the other: v = k·u for some k ≠ 0.

points.label: Scalar multiple
points.text: If u = (2, 3) and v = (6, 9), then v = 3u. They point in same direction (k > 0) or opposite (k < 0).

points.label: Coplanar vectors
points.text: Three vectors u, v, w are coplanar if they lie in the same plane. Equivalently, (u × v) · w = 0 (scalar triple product is zero).

example.problem: Are u = (1, 2, 3), v = (2, 4, 6), w = (1, 0, 1) coplanar? Check v = 2u (yes, collinear with u). So u and v don't span a plane. Now check if w is in the plane spanned by u and v. Since v = 2u, any point on their 'plane' is c₁u + c₂v = c₁u + 2c₂u = (c₁+2c₂)u. Can w = (1, 0, 1) be written as k(1, 2, 3)? If k(1, 2, 3) = (1, 0, 1), then k=1, 2k=0 (contradiction). So w is NOT coplanar.
example.solution: u and v are collinear (dependent), so they don't define a unique plane. w is linearly independent of them.

slides.inSimpleWords: Collinear vectors lie on one line. Coplanar vectors lie in one plane. Use scalar multiples and cross products to test.

slides.title: Projecting One Vector onto Another
slides.storyContext: Ramesh asks, 'If Kavya moves (3, 4) but we only count the eastward component, how far east did she go?' This is vector projection.

example.problem: Vector u = (3, 4). Project onto i-hat = (1, 0). Projection = (u · i-hat) i-hat = ((3, 4) · (1, 0)) (1, 0) = 3(1, 0) = (3, 0). Length of projection = 3.
example.solution: The eastward (x) component is 3 meters. Projection of u onto x-axis is (3, 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Project vector u onto direction v-hat (unit vector): proj = (u · v-hat) v-hat. The length is u · v-hat / |v|.

slides.title: Decomposing Movement into Parts
slides.storyContext: Pradeep shows Kavya how any movement can be broken into north-south and east-west parts. 'This decomposition is the foundation of vector mathematics. It simplifies complex movements.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Decompose vectors into components along coordinate axes. Makes calculations simpler and clearer.

slides.title: Linear Combinations of Vectors
slides.storyContext: Pradeep teaches Kavya about linear combinations: 'Any movement can be built by combining moves in the x and y directions.'

points.label: Linear combination
points.text: v = a₁u₁ + a₂u₂ + ... + aₙuₙ, where a₁, a₂, ... are scalars.

points.label: Basis vectors
points.text: In 2D, î = (1, 0) and ĵ = (0, 1) form a basis. Any 2D vector is v = vₓ î + vᵧ ĵ.

points.label: Linear dependence
points.text: Vectors u₁, u₂, ..., uₙ are linearly dependent if one can be written as a combination of others.

example.problem: Kavya's move: d = (3, 4). Write as linear combination of î and ĵ: d = 3î + 4ĵ. Now express using two other vectors: u = (1, 1), v = (1, −1). Solve: 3î + 4ĵ = a(1, 1) + b(1, −1) = (a+b, a−b). So a+b=3 and a−b=4. Adding: 2a=7, a=3.5. Then b=−0.5. Check: 3.5(1, 1) + (−0.5)(1, −1) = (3.5−0.5, 3.5+0.5) = (3, 4) ✓.
example.solution: d = 3.5u − 0.5v in the new basis. Linear combinations let us express vectors in different ways.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear combinations mix vectors with scalar weights. Basis vectors (like î, ĵ) span the entire space.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Parallel and Perpendicular Vectors
slides.storyContext: Kavya's teacher asks: if one dancer moves vector u = (2, 1) and another moves v = (4, 2), are they moving parallel? If a third moves w = (−1, 2), is w perpendicular to u?

points.text: Check if u and v are parallel: v = 2u? Yes. So parallel.
Check if u and w are perpendicular: u · w = 2(−1) + 1(2) = 0? Yes. So perpendicular.

example.problem: u = (2, 1), v = (4, 2), w = (−1, 2). Is v parallel to u? v = 2u ✓ (parallel). Is w ⊥ u? u · w = 2(−1) + 1(2) = −2 + 2 = 0 ✓ (perpendicular). Is w parallel to v? w = k·v means (−1, 2) = k(4, 2), so −1 = 4k, k = −1/4. Then 2 = 2k = −1/2 (false). Not parallel.
example.solution: u ∥ v (parallel). u ⊥ w (perpendicular). v ∦ w (not parallel).

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel if one is scalar multiple of the other. Perpendicular if dot product is zero.

slides.title: Full Problem: Group Dance Positioning
slides.storyContext: Ramesh choreographs a formation of four dancers. Kavya at A starts at center (0, 0). Three others start at B = (3, 4), C = (−2, 5), D = (4, −1) in meters. What's the center of mass of the group?

example.problem: Center of mass = (sum of position vectors) / (number of dancers) = (A + B + C + D) / 4 = [(0, 0) + (3, 4) + (−2, 5) + (4, −1)] / 4 = (5, 8) / 4 = (1.25, 2). Kavya confirms: the choreography centers around (1.25, 2), about 2.4 meters from stage center.
example.solution: Center of mass is at (1.25, 2). Ramesh uses this to plan the group's pivot point for synchronized turns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vector algebra helps choreograph group formations by calculating positions and centers.

slides.title: Magnitude as a Measure of Intensity
slides.storyContext: Pradeep explains: 'The magnitude of a force vector tells how strong the push is. A force of (3, 4) N has magnitude 5 N—that's the total push intensity.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnitude |v| = √(vₓ² + vᵧ² + v_z²) measures the 'strength' or 'intensity' of a vector quantity.

slides.title: Comparing Path and Displacement
slides.storyContext: Pradeep demonstrates why vectors matter: 'If Kavya walks 3 meters east, stops, then walks 4 meters north, she traveled 7 meters total. But her displacement—her actual change in position from start to end—is only 5 meters. Vectors capture the efficient path.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is path length; displacement is vector from start to finish. Vectors are more efficient for tracking positions.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Lift and Rotation
slides.storyContext: Two dancers: A at (0, 0) and B at (2, 3). They dance a move where A lifts B upward (in the z direction) by 1 meter, then they both rotate together. Use vectors to find B's new position.

points.text: Initial position of B: (2, 3, 0).
After lift: B moves to (2, 3, 1).
Find displacement, magnitude, and direction.

example.problem: Initial: B₀ = (2, 3, 0). Final: B₁ = (2, 3, 1). Displacement: Δr = B₁ − B₀ = (0, 0, 1). Magnitude: |Δr| = 1 meter (pure vertical lift). Direction: straight up (along k̂).
example.solution: The lift moves B vertically 1 meter. B ends at (2, 3, 1), now 1 meter higher while maintaining horizontal position.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use vector subtraction to track movement in 3D space during complex choreography.

slides.title: Vector Magnitude in 3D
slides.storyContext: Pradeep extends magnitude to 3D: 'For spatial movements with height, width, and depth, magnitude is |v| = √(vₓ² + vᵧ² + v_z²).'

points.label: 3D magnitude formula
points.text: |v| = √(vₓ² + vᵧ² + v_z²). This is Pythagoras extended to 3 dimensions.

points.label: Unit sphere
points.text: All vectors with magnitude 1 form a unit sphere centered at origin.

example.problem: Lift vector: v = (0, 0, 1). Magnitude = √(0² + 0² + 1²) = 1. Spatial move: w = (3, 4, 5). Magnitude = √(9 + 16 + 25) = √50 ≈ 7.07.
example.solution: 3D magnitude generalizes 2D formula. Longer movements in multiple directions have larger magnitude.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D magnitude = √(x² + y² + z²). It's the Euclidean distance from origin to the point (x, y, z).

slides.title: Combining Concepts: Real Dance Choreography
slides.storyContext: Pradeep helps Ramesh choreograph a finale: Kavya starts at (0, 0), moves by vector v₁ = (5, 0) (5 m east). Then adds v₂ = (3, 4) (3 m east, 4 m north). Finally, she rotates her body (angular momentum from cross product). Calculate her final position and the angle of that final movement.

example.problem: Final position: (0, 0) + (5, 0) + (3, 4) = (8, 4). Total displacement v = (8, 4). Magnitude |v| = √64 + 16 = √80 = 4√5 ≈ 8.94 m. Direction: θ = arctan(4/8) = arctan(1/2) ≈ 26.6° north of east.
example.solution: Kavya ends 8.94 meters away from start, 26.6° north of east. This is the net effect of all her moves combined.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vector algebra lets you combine multiple moves into one final position, saving calculations.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Scalars are just numbers; vectors have magnitude and direction.
Components: v = (vₓ, vᵧ, v_z) or v = vₓ î + vᵧ ĵ + v_z k̂.
Vector addition: add components separately.
Dot product u·v = |u| |v| cos(θ). Zero if perpendicular.
Cross product u × v is perpendicular to both, magnitude |u| |v| sin(θ).
Unit vectors: divide by magnitude. Direction cosines: cos(α), cos(β), cos(γ) with sum of squares = 1.
Collinear vectors lie on one line; coplanar vectors lie in one plane.
Linear combinations build any vector from basis vectors.
Applications: displacement, force, work, torque, positioning in 3D space.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vectors describe position, movement, force, and rotation in space—essential for physics and engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: Akshay's Construction: Building in 3D Space
hook: An architect learns to work in three dimensions using coordinate geometry

slides.title: Three Dimensional Geometry
slides.storyContext: Akshay interns at an architecture firm in Mumbai. His first project: design a small pavilion. The architects use 3D coordinates to plan every beam, column, and roof angle. 'Geometry isn't flat,' Rukhsana tells him. 'It's three-dimensional, and math is the blueprint.'

slides.title: The Pavilion Blueprint
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana sketches a pavilion with four corners. She places the origin (0, 0, 0) at ground level, center. Corners are at A(2, 2, 0), B(−2, 2, 0), C(−2, −2, 0), D(2, −2, 0). Four columns rise at each corner to height 4 meters: A'(2, 2, 4), B'(−2, 2, 4), C'(−2, −2, 4), D'(2, −2, 4). A roof beam connects A' to C'. Akshay asks, 'How do I describe this in math?' Vikram (his friend who's good at geometry) says, 'With 3D coordinates, lines, planes, and distances.'

slides.title: 3D Coordinate System and Distance
slides.storyContext: Vikram teaches Akshay the 3D Cartesian system: three perpendicular axes (x, y, z) with origin O(0, 0, 0). Every point P is (x, y, z).

points.label: 3D Coordinates
points.text: Point P(x, y, z): x is distance along x-axis, y along y-axis, z (height) along z-axis.

points.label: Distance formula
points.text: Distance between P₁(x₁, y₁, z₁) and P₂(x₂, y₂, z₂) is d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²].

points.label: Section formula
points.text: Point dividing line segment P₁P₂ in ratio m:n is R = ((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂+ny₁)/(m+n), (mz₂+nz₁)/(m+n)).

example.solution: Roof beam is 4√2 ≈ 5.66 m long and its midpoint is at ground center, 4 m high.

slides.inSimpleWords: In 3D, use (x, y, z) to place points. Distance is found by extending the 2D formula to three dimensions.

slides.title: Measuring Diagonals
slides.storyContext: Akshay needs to know the diagonal from ground corner A(2, 2, 0) to roof corner C'(−2, −2, 4). This is a major bracing element.

example.solution: The diagonal is about 6.93 meters—a key measurement for structural stability.

slides.inSimpleWords: Large diagonals across buildings help brace the structure and distribute weight.

slides.title: Direction Cosines and Ratios
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana points to a diagonal beam and asks Akshay, 'At what angles does this beam make with the x, y, z axes?' This is where direction cosines come in.

points.label: Direction cosines
points.text: For line from P₁(x₁, y₁, z₁) to P₂(x₂, y₂, z₂): direction numbers are (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁, z₂−z₁). Direction cosines are (cos α, cos β, cos γ), where cos α = (x₂−x₁)/d, etc., and d is distance.

points.label: Identity
points.text: cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1.

points.label: Direction ratios
points.text: Often write as a:b:c (proportional to x-difference, y-difference, z-difference). Simplify by finding GCD.

example.problem: Diagonal column from A'(2, 2, 4) to opposite base corner C(−2, −2, 0). Direction numbers: (−2−2, −2−2, 0−4) = (−4, −4, −4) or simplified (−1, −1, −1) or (1, 1, 1). Distance = √(16 + 16 + 16) = √48 = 4√3. Direction cosines: cos α = −4/(4√3) = −1/√3, cos β = −1/√3, cos γ = −4/(4√3) = −1/√3. Verify: (−1/√3)² + (−1/√3)² + (−1/√3)² = 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1. ✓
example.solution: Direction ratios (1:1:1). Direction cosines (−1/√3, −1/√3, −1/√3), meaning the diagonal makes equal angles with all three axes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines tell the angles a line makes with x, y, z axes. They always sum (as squares) to 1.

slides.title: Thinking About Beam Directions
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana explains to Akshay: 'Every structural element has a direction. Columns go mostly vertical (high z component). Horizontal beams have low z. Know the direction, and you can calculate stresses accurately.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Direction determines how forces and stresses act on structural elements. Always specify direction in designs.

slides.title: Equation of a Line in 3D
slides.storyContext: Vikram shows Akshay how to write the equation of any line in space—essential for specifying beams and columns in the design.

points.label: Vector form
points.text: Line through point P₀(x₀, y₀, z₀) with direction ratios a:b:c is r = r₀ + t(a, b, c), where r₀ = (x₀, y₀, z₀) and t is parameter.

points.label: Parametric form
points.text: x = x₀ + at, y = y₀ + bt, z = z₀ + ct (t is parameter, can be any real number).

points.label: Symmetric form
points.text: (x − x₀)/a = (y − y₀)/b = (z − z₀)/c (requires a, b, c ≠ 0).

example.problem: Pavilion column from A(2, 2, 0) to A'(2, 2, 4). Direction: (0, 0, 4) or (0, 0, 1). Parametric: x = 2, y = 2, z = 0 + 1·t = t (for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4). Symmetric form: This is degenerate since x and y don't change. Better written as x = 2, y = 2, 0 ≤ z ≤ 4.
example.solution: Column equation: x = 2, y = 2, 0 ≤ z ≤ 4. It's a vertical line at (2, 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: A line in 3D needs a starting point and a direction. Parametric equations let you find any point on the line.

slides.title: Roof Beam Parametric Equation
slides.storyContext: Akshay needs the parametric equation of the roof beam from A'(2, 2, 4) to C'(−2, −2, 4).

example.solution: Roof beam: x = 2−t, y = 2−t, z = 4. It stays at height 4 while moving diagonally across the pavilion.

slides.inSimpleWords: When both start and end points are known, direction = end − start.

slides.title: Finding Midpoints and Divisions
slides.storyContext: Akshay needs to place a support column at the midpoint of a diagonal. Rukhsana explains: 'Use the section formula. If a beam goes from (2, 2, 4) to (−2, −2, 4), the midpoint is the average of coordinates.'

example.problem: Beam from A'(2, 2, 4) to C'(−2, −2, 4). Midpoint: M = ((2−2)/2, (2−2)/2, (4+4)/2) = (0, 0, 4). This is ground center at roof height.
example.solution: Support column should be placed at (0, 0, 4)—the geometric center of the roof beam.

slides.inSimpleWords: Midpoint = average of endpoints. Use for centering supports and measuring beam halves.

slides.title: Equation of a Plane
slides.storyContext: The roof of the pavilion is a flat plane. Rukhsana asks Akshay to describe its equation. This plane passes through four points at height z = 4.

points.label: General equation
points.text: Plane equation: ax + by + cz + d = 0, where (a, b, c) is normal vector to the plane.

points.label: Point-normal form
points.text: Plane through P₀(x₀, y₀, z₀) with normal (a, b, c): a(x − x₀) + b(y − y₀) + c(z − z₀) = 0.

points.label: Intercept form
points.text: Plane with x-intercept a, y-intercept b, z-intercept c: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.

example.problem: Roof plane passes through A'(2, 2, 4), B'(−2, 2, 4), C'(−2, −2, 4), D'(2, −2, 4). All have z = 4. Normal vector points vertically: (0, 0, 1). Plane equation: 0(x − 0) + 0(y − 0) + 1(z − 4) = 0, so z = 4. Or general form: 0x + 0y + 1z − 4 = 0.
example.solution: Roof plane equation is z = 4. Any point on the roof has height exactly 4 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: A plane is defined by ax + by + cz + d = 0. The coefficients (a, b, c) are the normal direction perpendicular to the plane.

slides.title: Vertical and Slanted Planes
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana shows Akshay the difference: roof at z = 4 is horizontal (normal pointing straight up). But a slanted wall might have normal (1, 0, 1)—tilted toward one side.

example.problem: Horizontal roof: z = 4 (normal (0, 0, 1)). Slanted wall passing through origin with normal (1, 0, 1): 1(x) + 0(y) + 1(z) = 0, or x + z = 0.
example.solution: Horizontal and slanted planes have different normal vectors pointing in different directions.

slides.inSimpleWords: The normal vector (a, b, c) defines the plane's orientation. Different normals mean different tilt angles.

slides.title: Angle Between Lines and Planes
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana needs to know: (1) at what angle does a bracing diagonal meet a column? (2) at what angle does a slanted beam meet the roof plane?

points.label: Angle between two lines
points.text: Lines with direction ratios a₁:b₁:c₁ and a₂:b₂:c₂. cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / √(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²) √(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²).

points.label: Angle between line and plane
points.text: Line with direction (a, b, c); plane with normal (p, q, r). sin φ = |ap + bq + cr| / √(a² + b² + c²) √(p² + q² + r²).

points.label: Perpendicularity
points.text: Lines perpendicular if a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0. Line perpendicular to plane if (a, b, c) parallel to (p, q, r).

example.solution: The diagonal meets the column at about 54.7°. Structural engineers use this to calculate stresses.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles between lines and planes are found using dot products of direction and normal vectors.

slides.title: Angle Between Two Beams
slides.storyContext: Two bracing beams: one from A(2, 2, 0) toward D'(2, −2, 4), another from B(−2, 2, 0) toward A'(2, 2, 4). What angle do they make?

example.solution: The two beams meet at 60°—a good angle for structural rigidity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use direction vectors and dot product to find angles between any two lines or beams.

slides.title: Distance from Point to Plane
slides.storyContext: Akshay asks: 'If a support point is at (1, 1, 2) and the roof is at z = 4, how far away is it?' This is point-to-plane distance.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Distance from P(x₀, y₀, z₀) to plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is: dist = |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d| / √(a² + b² + c²).

points.label: Special case
points.text: If plane is z = k, distance from (x₀, y₀, z₀) is simply |z₀ − k|.

example.problem: Point (1, 1, 2) to roof plane z = 4. Distance = |2 − 4| = 2 meters. Alternatively, plane is 0x + 0y + 1z − 4 = 0. Distance = |0(1) + 0(1) + 1(2) − 4| / √(0 + 0 + 1) = |2 − 4| / 1 = 2.
example.solution: Support point is 2 meters below the roof—room for a truss.

slides.inSimpleWords: Point-to-plane distance measures how far a point is from a plane, perpendicular to the plane.

slides.title: Full Problem: Roof Truss Design
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana designs a roof truss connecting two opposite roof corners A'(2, 2, 4) and C'(−2, −2, 4), with a central support at height 5 meters directly above the origin: S(0, 0, 5). Find (a) lengths of the two diagonal braces A'S and C'S, (b) equation of plane containing A', C', S, and (c) check if all three points are coplanar.

example.solution: Both diagonal braces are 3 meters long. The plane containing A', C', S is y = x. This defines the symmetry plane of the truss.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry lets architects design complex structures by calculating distances, angles, and plane equations.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Corner Brace
slides.storyContext: A corner brace runs from A(2, 2, 0) to A'(2, 2, 4) and then to S(0, 0, 5). Find (a) total length of this path, (b) the straight-line distance from A to S.

points.text: (a) Length A to A' plus A' to S.
(b) Direct distance from A to S.

example.solution: Path length is 7 m; direct distance is √33 ≈ 5.74 m (shorter, as expected).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use distance formula repeatedly for paths with multiple segments.

slides.title: Setting Up Coordinate Systems in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Vikram explains: 'Choose origin wisely—usually the center of the building or a corner. Then align x, y, z with the building's main directions (length, width, height).'
slides.inSimpleWords: Smart coordinate choice makes calculations simple. Place origin at a natural center or corner, not randomly.

slides.title: Distance Between Two Lines in 3D
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana asks: 'If two crossing beams don't touch, how close do they come?' This is the distance between skew lines.

points.label: Skew lines
points.text: Two lines that don't intersect and aren't parallel. In 3D, non-parallel lines often don't meet.

points.label: Shortest distance
points.text: Distance between lines through P₁, P₂ with directions d₁, d₂ is: dist = |(P₂ − P₁) · (d₁ × d₂)| / |d₁ × d₂|.

example.problem: Line 1: A(2, 2, 0) in direction (0, 0, 1). Line 2: C(−2, −2, 0) in direction (0, 0, 1). Both vertical! d₁ = (0, 0, 1), d₂ = (0, 0, 1). Cross product d₁ × d₂ = 0 (parallel). Distance between parallel lines = distance from A to line 2 = √[(−2−2)² + (−2−2)²] = √32 = 4√2 ≈ 5.66 m.
example.solution: The two vertical columns are 5.66 meters apart—the diagonal of the pavilion base.

slides.inSimpleWords: Skew lines don't meet. Use cross product to find the closest distance between them.

slides.title: Where Walls Meet the Roof
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana points out that every edge where a wall meets the roof is an intersection of two planes. 'Understanding these intersections is key to architectural drawings,' she tells Akshay.
slides.inSimpleWords: Plane intersections define edges and boundaries in 3D buildings. Always solve plane systems to find these edges.

slides.title: Planes and Intersections
slides.storyContext: Two walls (planes) meet along a line. Rukhsana wants to know where.

points.label: Plane intersection
points.text: Two planes intersect (if not parallel) along a line. Solve system of two plane equations to find line.

points.label: Three planes
points.text: Three planes can intersect at a point (if not parallel/dependent). Solve system of three plane equations.

example.problem: Roof plane: z = 4. South wall: y = 2. Intersection? Substitute y = 2 and z = 4 into the space. We get points (x, 2, 4) for any x. This is a line: the southern edge of the roof.
example.solution: The line is (x, 2, 4)—parametric form: (t, 2, 4) for any t. It's a horizontal line along the roof's south edge.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two planes intersect in a line (if not parallel). Find the line by solving both plane equations together.

slides.title: Symmetry in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Akshay notices that the pavilion is symmetric: the plane y = x divides it into two mirror halves. 'Planes define symmetry,' Vikram explains. 'In design, symmetry is both beautiful and structurally sound.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry planes simplify calculations. If a structure mirrors across a plane, calculations only needed for one half.

slides.title: Finding Where Three Planes Meet
slides.storyContext: Three structural walls define planes: east face (x = 2), north face (y = 2), and roof (z = 4). They meet at a single corner. Solve the system to find it.

example.problem: Planes: x = 2, y = 2, z = 4. All three simultaneously: x=2 AND y=2 AND z=4. Solution: unique point (2, 2, 4). This is corner A'.
example.solution: Three planes intersect at a single point (2, 2, 4). In general, three planes generically intersect at a point (unless dependent or parallel).

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve system of 3 plane equations to find their common point. Use substitution or elimination.

slides.title: Visualizing 3D from 2D Drawings
slides.storyContext: Vikram teaches Akshay: 'Architects use 2D projections (top view, front view, side view). But the reality is 3D. Coordinate geometry bridges them. Each 2D projection is a slice of 3D space.'
slides.inSimpleWords: 3D coordinates let you convert between multiple 2D views (projections) of one building. Essential for engineering drawings.

slides.title: Verifying the Pavilion Design
slides.storyContext: Before construction, Rukhsana verifies all measurements are consistent. She checks: are the four ground corners equidistant from origin? Do all roof corners have the same height?

example.problem: Ground corners: A(2,2,0), B(-2,2,0), C(-2,-2,0), D(2,-2,0). Distance from origin: |A|=√(4+4)=√8=2√2. Same for B, C, D ✓. Roof corners: A'(2,2,4), B'(-2,2,4), C'(-2,-2,4), D'(2,-2,4). Heights: all z=4 ✓. Verification passed.
example.solution: Symmetry verified. All corners equidistant and level. Pavilion is balanced.

slides.inSimpleWords: Verify designs by checking distances and heights consistently. Catch errors before construction.

slides.title: Real-World Precision
slides.storyContext: Akshay realizes: 'One small mistake in a coordinate, and the whole building could be crooked. That's why mathematics is so important in construction. Millimeters matter.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Coordinate geometry ensures precision. Architecture demands mathematical rigor. Tiny errors scale to massive problems.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) locate points in space.
Distance: d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²].
Lines: parametric (x=x₀+at, y=y₀+bt, z=z₀+ct) or symmetric ((x−x₀)/a = (y−y₀)/b = (z−z₀)/c).
Planes: ax + by + cz + d = 0. Normal vector (a, b, c) is perpendicular to plane.
Direction cosines satisfy cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1.
Angle between lines uses dot product of direction vectors.
Angle between line and plane uses dot product of line direction and plane normal.
Distance from point to plane: |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d| / √(a² + b² + c²).
Applications: building design, structural engineering, astronomy, navigation.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry is the mathematical language of architecture and engineering. Coordinate systems, lines, and planes define space.

image.alt: What We Learned — Three Dimensional Geometry

subject: Mathematics
title: Sophia's Bakery: Maximizing Profit
hook: A baker uses linear programming to decide what to bake for maximum profit

slides.title: Linear Programming
slides.storyContext: Sophia opens a small bakery in Delhi. Every day she has limited flour, butter, and oven time. Some days she bakes bread; other days, cakes. She wants maximum profit. Her brother Rahul says, 'This is a math problem'—it's linear programming.

slides.title: The Bakery Decision
slides.storyContext: Each day Sophia has: 10 kg flour, 2 kg butter. Bread uses 1 kg flour, 0.25 kg butter, takes 20 min, sells for ₹250 profit. Cake uses 1 kg flour, 0.5 kg butter, takes 30 min, sells for ₹400 profit. Oven capacity is 3 hours (180 min). How many breads and cakes should Sophia make to maximize profit? Rahul sketches constraints on a board. Ms. Chopra explains, 'This is linear programming—you have variables, constraints, and an objective to maximize.'

slides.title: What is Linear Programming?
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra starts the lesson. 'Linear programming solves real-world optimization problems where we have limited resources and want to maximize or minimize an outcome.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Linear Programming Problem (LPP): optimize (maximize or minimize) a linear objective function subject to linear constraints (inequalities or equalities) and non-negativity conditions.

points.label: Objective function
points.text: z = c₁x₁ + c₂x₂ + ... + cₙxₙ (profit, cost, etc. to optimize).

points.label: Constraints
points.text: Linear inequalities like a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ ≤ b (resource limits). Non-negativity: x₁, x₂, ... ≥ 0 (can't make negative items).

points.label: Feasible region
points.text: Set of all (x₁, x₂, ...) satisfying all constraints. Graphically, it's a polygon (in 2D) or polytope (in 3D+).

example.problem: Sophia's LPP: Let x = breads, y = cakes. Objective: maximize Z = 250x + 400y (profit). Constraints: (1) 1x + 1y ≤ 10 (flour), (2) 0.25x + 0.5y ≤ 2 (butter), (3) 20x + 30y ≤ 180 (oven time), (4) x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negativity).
example.solution: This LPP describes Sophia's daily baking decision. The solution will be a point (x, y) where profit is highest while respecting all limits.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming finds the best combination of decisions when resources are limited and outcomes are proportional to decisions.

image.alt: What is Linear Programming? — Linear Programming

slides.title: Formulating the Problem
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra walks Sophia through formulation: 'First, define decision variables (what you control). Then, state your objective (what you want to optimize). Finally, list all constraints (what limits you).'

example.problem: Variables: x = loaves of bread, y = cakes. Objective: Z = 250x + 400y (maximize profit in rupees). Constraints: flour (x + y ≤ 10), butter (0.25x + 0.5y ≤ 2), time (20x + 30y ≤ 180), non-negative (x, y ≥ 0).
example.solution: A clear formulation is half the battle. Sophia now has a precise mathematical model.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every optimization problem needs: (1) variables (decision choices), (2) objective (goal), (3) constraints (limits).

slides.title: Graphical Method (2D Problems)
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra draws the constraints on a graph. She shows Sophia how to find the feasible region—the polygon where all constraints are satisfied.

points.label: Step 1: Plot constraints
points.text: Draw each inequality as a boundary line. Shade the region where the inequality holds.

points.label: Step 2: Find feasible region
points.text: Intersection of all shaded regions is the feasible region (usually a convex polygon).

points.label: Step 3: Find corner points
points.text: Optimal solution lies at a corner (vertex) of the feasible polygon. Find all corner points.

points.label: Step 4: Evaluate objective
points.text: Calculate objective function Z at each corner. Maximum (or minimum) Z is the optimal value.

example.problem: Sophia's constraints: (1) x + y ≤ 10, (2) 0.25x + 0.5y ≤ 2 (rewrite: x + 2y ≤ 8), (3) 20x + 30y ≤ 180 (rewrite: 2x + 3y ≤ 18). Corner points: O(0, 0), A(0, 4), B(2, 3), C(4, 2). Evaluate Z = 250x + 400y: Z(O)=0, Z(A)=1600, Z(B)=1700, Z(C)=1800. Maximum is ₹1800 at C(4, 2).
example.solution: Optimal: 4 breads, 2 cakes, profit ₹1800.

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw constraints, find the feasible polygon, check corners, and pick the corner with highest (or lowest) objective value.

slides.title: Graphing Constraints Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra carefully draws each constraint line to show Sophia the feasible region.

example.problem: Constraint 1: x + y = 10 (line from (10, 0) to (0, 10)). Shade below (x + y ≤ 10). Constraint 2: x + 2y = 8 (line from (8, 0) to (0, 4)). Shade below (x + 2y ≤ 8). Constraint 3: 2x + 3y = 18 (line from (9, 0) to (0, 6)). Shade below (2x + 3y ≤ 18). Non-negativity: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (shade in first quadrant). The overlapping region is a quadrilateral.
example.solution: Visual inspection of the graph shows which corner likely has maximum profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphing makes the problem visible. The feasible region is where all shaded areas overlap.

slides.title: Corner Points and Optimality
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra explains why corners matter: 'In linear programming, the optimal solution is always at a corner (vertex) of the feasible region. This is because linear objectives increase in a single direction.'

points.label: Fundamental theorem
points.text: If an LPP has an optimal solution, it exists at a corner of the feasible region.

points.label: Why corners?
points.text: The objective function Z = 250x + 400y is linear. Level curves (lines of constant Z) are parallel. The last level curve touching the feasible region touches at a corner.

example.problem: Profit lines for Sophia: Z = 0, Z = 1000, Z = 1500, Z = 1800, ... These are lines: 250x + 400y = Z. Higher Z means lines further from origin. As Z increases, the line slides up and right. It last touches the feasible region at corner C(4, 2), where Z = 1800.
example.solution: By the fundamental theorem, the optimal corner is C(4, 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Optimal solutions occur at corners because objective lines are parallel and slide across the region.

slides.title: Checking Multiple Corners
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra emphasizes: 'Never assume the first good-looking corner is optimal. Always calculate Z at every corner. The global optimum might be at a corner you overlooked.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exhaustively check all corners of the feasible region. The optimum is guaranteed to be at one of them.

slides.title: Standard Form and Canonical Form
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra teaches Sophia how to convert any LPP into a standard form suitable for computer algorithms (like the simplex method).

points.label: Standard form
points.text: All constraints are ≤ inequalities (for maximization) or ≥ (for minimization). All variables ≥ 0. Objective is maximize or minimize. All constants on RHS ≥ 0.

points.label: Canonical form
points.text: Convert inequalities to equalities by adding slack variables (for ≤) or surplus variables (for ≥). Slack sᵢ ≥ 0; surplus eᵢ ≥ 0.

points.label: Slack variable example
points.text: Constraint x + y ≤ 10 becomes x + y + s = 10 (s ≥ 0 is unused resource).

points.label: Surplus variable example
points.text: Constraint 2x + y ≥ 8 becomes 2x + y − e = 8 (e ≥ 0 is excess).

example.problem: Sophia's LPP in canonical form: Maximize Z = 250x + 400y. Subject to: x + y + s₁ = 10, x + 2y + s₂ = 8, 2x + 3y + s₃ = 18, x, y, s₁, s₂, s₃ ≥ 0. Here, s₁ = unused flour capacity, s₂ = unused butter capacity, s₃ = unused oven time.
example.solution: In canonical form, the problem is ready for simplex method or matrix algorithms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slack variables represent unused resources. Converting to canonical form makes the problem solvable by algorithms.

image.alt: Standard Form and Canonical Form — Linear Programming

slides.title: Unbounded and Infeasible Solutions
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra warns Sophia, 'Not all LPPs have a solution. Sometimes the feasible region is empty (infeasible). Other times, profit can grow infinitely (unbounded).'

points.label: Feasible region
points.text: Must be non-empty for a solution to exist. If constraints contradict (e.g., x ≥ 10 and x ≤ 5), problem is infeasible.

points.label: Unbounded solution
points.text: If feasible region extends to infinity in direction of objective improvement, optimal value is unbounded (e.g., 'profit → ∞ as production → ∞').

points.label: Degenerate solution
points.text: If two or more constraints are tight (active) at optimal point, solution is degenerate.

example.problem: Example of infeasible: x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3, x + y ≤ 7. No point satisfies all three (5 + 3 = 8 > 7). Example of unbounded: maximize Z = 2x + 3y subject to x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (no upper limit). As x, y → ∞, Z → ∞.
example.solution: Sophia's bakery problem is neither unbounded nor infeasible because resources (flour, butter, time) are finite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always check if the feasible region exists and is bounded. Bad inputs lead to infeasible or unbounded problems.

slides.title: Sensitivity Analysis
slides.storyContext: Sophia asks, 'What if butter prices change? What if I can get more oven time? How does my answer change?' This is sensitivity analysis.

points.label: Shadow price (dual value)
points.text: Marginal value of one unit of a resource. If flour's shadow price is ₹50, producing 1 more bread (using 1 kg flour) increases profit by ₹50.

points.label: Range of feasibility
points.text: Range of RHS values (resource amount) over which optimal basis remains valid.

points.label: Range of optimality
points.text: Range of objective coefficients (prices) over which current solution remains optimal.

example.problem: Suppose Sophia's optimal is 4 breads, 2 cakes (profit ₹1800). Shadow price of flour = ₹100 means: if she gets 11 kg flour instead of 10, new profit ≈ ₹1900. Shadow price of butter = ₹300 means: if she gets 2.5 kg butter, profit ≈ ₹1950.
example.solution: Sensitivity analysis helps Sophia decide if buying extra butter (at a cost) is worth it. If butter costs ₹200/kg and shadow price is ₹300/kg, buy more!

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadow prices tell how profit changes when resource amounts change. Use them to decide if investing in more resources pays off.

slides.title: Identifying the Binding Constraint
slides.storyContext: At the optimal point (4 breads, 2 cakes), Sophia checks which resources are fully used. Butter: 1 + 1 = 2 kg (all used). Flour: 4 + 2 = 6 kg (only 6 of 10 used). Time: 80 + 60 = 140 min (only 140 of 180 used). Butter is the bottleneck!
slides.inSimpleWords: The binding constraint (fully used resource) limits profit most. Invest in increasing it first.

slides.title: Full Solution: Sophia's Optimal Production
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra walks Sophia through the complete graphical solution. She finds all corner points of the feasible region and calculates profit at each.

example.problem: Feasible corners (verified): O(0, 0), A(0, 4), B(2, 3), C(4, 2). Profits: Z(O) = 0, Z(A) = 250·0 + 400·4 = 1600, Z(B) = 250·2 + 400·3 = 500 + 1200 = 1700, Z(C) = 250·4 + 400·2 = 1000 + 800 = 1800. Maximum is at C(4, 2) with profit ₹1800. Resource usage at C: flour = 4 + 2 = 6 kg (4 unused), butter = 1 + 1 = 2 kg (fully used), time = 80 + 60 = 140 min (40 unused).
example.solution: Sophia should bake 4 breads and 2 cakes daily to maximize profit at ₹1800. Butter is the binding constraint. If she wants more profit, she should invest in more butter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphical method finds the optimal corner by checking each vertex of the feasible region.

slides.title: Test Yourself: New Product
slides.storyContext: Sophia introduces pastries: 0.5 kg flour, 0.25 kg butter, 15 min oven, ₹300 profit. Formulate and solve the new LPP with x breads, y cakes, z pastries.

points.text: Objective: maximize Z = 250x + 400y + 300z.
Constraints: flour, butter, time, non-negativity.

example.problem: Constraints: 1x + 1y + 0.5z ≤ 10 (flour), 0.25x + 0.5y + 0.25z ≤ 2 (butter), 20x + 30y + 15z ≤ 180 (time), x,y,z ≥ 0. This is a 3-variable problem; graphical solution is hard (3D polytope). Use simplex method or software.
example.solution: With 3 variables, graphical method isn't practical. Use simplex method or linear programming software (Excel Solver, Python PuLP, etc.).

slides.inSimpleWords: For 3+ variables, graphical method becomes impractical. Use algorithms (simplex) or software.

slides.title: Real-World Impact
slides.storyContext: Sophia implements the solution: every day, bake 4 breads and 2 cakes. Within a month, profit is steady at ₹1800/day. Her revenue rises from ₹1200/day (old haphazard plan) to ₹1800/day. Linear programming saved her ₹18,000 in a month!
slides.inSimpleWords: Mathematical optimization directly translates to business success. Better decisions = more profit.

slides.title: Minimization vs Maximization
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra contrasts: 'We maximized Sophia's profit. But a factory might minimize production cost. The method is identical—only the objective changes.'

points.label: Maximization
points.text: Maximize Z = c₁x₁ + c₂x₂ + ... (e.g., profit). Optimal corner is where Z is largest.

points.label: Minimization
points.text: Minimize Z = c₁x₁ + c₂x₂ + ... (e.g., cost). Optimal corner is where Z is smallest.

example.problem: Diet problem: minimize cost of meals. Constraints: nutrition requirements (protein ≥ 50g, carbs ≥ 200g, etc.). Variables: amount of each food. Corners of feasible region are checked; minimum cost corner is optimal.
example.solution: Minimization uses the same graphical and simplex methods as maximization.

slides.inSimpleWords: Maximization and minimization are structurally identical. Only the objective direction differs.

slides.title: When Constraints Compete
slides.storyContext: Sophia realizes butter is the binding constraint—she's using all 2 kg. 'If I buy more butter, I could bake more cakes. But should I?' Ms. Chopra explains shadow prices: butter's marginal value is ₹300/kg. If butter costs ₹150/kg wholesale, buying extra is profitable.
slides.inSimpleWords: When two or more constraints are equally tight, they jointly limit profit. Break the tightest one first for fastest gains.

slides.title: Simplex Method (Brief Introduction)
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra sketches the simplex algorithm: 'For 3+ variables, graphical method doesn't work. Simplex starts at one corner, moves to a better corner, and repeats until no better corner exists.'

points.label: Iterative improvement
points.text: Simplex moves from corner to corner, always toward improving objective.

points.label: Pivot operation
points.text: At each step, swap a basic variable for a non-basic one; recalculate objective.

points.label: Termination
points.text: Stop when no neighboring corner improves objective (optimality reached).

example.problem: For 3-variable problem (breads, cakes, pastries), simplex would start at corner O(0,0,0), then move through sequence of corners (each calculated) until reaching optimal. Unlike graphical method, doesn't require visualizing feasible polytope.
example.solution: Simplex is automated; computers use it for real problems. We understand graphical method for intuition; algorithms handle complexity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Simplex method is automated corner-hopping for 3+ variables. Graphical method is intuition; simplex is brute-force precision.

slides.title: Real Industrial Problems
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra shares: 'Air India uses LP to schedule flights and crew. Pharma companies use it to allocate production across facilities. Retailers use it for inventory and pricing. LP is everywhere.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming powers decisions in airlines, manufacturing, retail, logistics. Scale from bakery to billions.

slides.title: Duality in Linear Programming
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra introduces duality: 'For every LPP (primal), there's a related problem (dual). Solving one gives insights into the other. Shadow prices come from the dual.'

points.label: Primal problem
points.text: Maximize profit. Variables = production quantities. Constraints = resources.

points.label: Dual problem
points.text: Minimize resource cost. Variables = shadow prices (resource values). Constraints = product profitability.

points.label: Duality insight
points.text: Optimal primal value = optimal dual value. Resources are priced implicitly by the dual.

example.problem: Sophia's primal: max 250x + 400y subject to flour, butter, time. Dual: min 10w₁ + 2w₂ + 180w₃ subject to w₁ + 0.25w₂ + 20w₃ ≥ 250 (bread), w₁ + 0.5w₂ + 30w₃ ≥ 400 (cake). w₁, w₂, w₃ are shadow prices of flour, butter, time. Optimal dual value = ₹1800 (same as primal).
example.solution: Duality reveals that resources can be valued as shadow prices. If shadow price of butter is ₹300/kg and market price is ₹150/kg, buying is a bargain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dual problem values resources. Primal maximizes production; dual minimizes resource cost. Both have same optimal value.

slides.title: Scaling to Reality
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra explains: 'This simple 2-variable problem is just a start. Real bakeries have dozens of products, seasonal demands, quality constraints, and logistics. But the principles remain: formulate, constrain, optimize.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming scales from toy problems to massive industrial decisions. The method is universal.

slides.title: Testing Infeasibility and Unboundedness
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra poses hypotheticals: 'What if Sophia had contradictory demands? Or what if she had unlimited resources? Let's recognize these red flags.'

example.problem: Infeasible case: x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 10. No solution (10 > 5). Unbounded case: max 2x + 3y subject to x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (no upper limit). Profit → ∞.
example.solution: Always check: does feasible region exist? Is it bounded? Infeasible or unbounded problems need remodeling.

slides.inSimpleWords: Catch bad model setups early. Test for infeasibility (contradictory constraints) and unboundedness (missing limits).

slides.title: Post-Optimality Decisions
slides.storyContext: After finding the optimal solution (4 breads, 2 cakes), Sophia asks: 'What if a supplier raises flour prices? What if a competitor captures cake demand, so I get less profit per cake?' These are post-optimality questions.
slides.inSimpleWords: After optimizing, ask how robust the solution is. Will small changes to costs or demands break your strategy?

slides.title: Verifying Feasibility at Optimal Point
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra double-checks Sophia's optimal solution (4, 2) satisfies all constraints.

example.solution: Solution (4, 2) is feasible and gives profit ₹1800. Verified.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always verify the proposed solution satisfies all constraints and achieves the objective.

slides.title: From Theory to Practice
slides.storyContext: Sophia implements the solution and within weeks sees profit increase. 'Math isn't just theory,' she tells Ms. Chopra. 'It's real money in my pocket.' Ms. Chopra smiles: 'That's the power of optimization.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming bridges mathematics and business reality. Correct decisions lead to measurable success.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Linear Programming optimizes (maximize or minimize) a linear objective subject to linear constraints.
Feasible region: set of all solutions satisfying all constraints. Optimal solution lies at a corner.
Graphical method works for 2D. List all corners, evaluate objective at each, pick best.
Standard form: all ≤ constraints (or ≥), all variables ≥ 0, RHS ≥ 0.
Canonical form: convert ≤ to = by adding slack variables.
Shadow prices: marginal value of resources. Help decide if buying more resources is profitable.
Sensitivity analysis: how does solution change if parameters change?
Applications: production planning, diet problems, transportation, resource allocation, business strategy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming is the math of optimal resource allocation. Find the corner of the feasible region with the best objective value.
